nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the prolific popular novelist of the working woman and the anarchist's travel books
literary_identity: Novelist and travel writer; the author of Sounding Brass and Ragged Banners.
biography: Born Ethel Edith Mannin in London on 6 October 1900, the daughter of a postal worker; she left school at fifteen, worked in a pension office and in advertising before Sounding Brass (1926) began a career of more than a hundred books - a novel and a non-fiction book a year. Her early novels of the working woman, her autobiography Confessions and Impressions (1930), her anarchism and her anti-fascism made her a popular and committed voice of the decades; she died at Teignmouth on 5 December 1984.
literary_profile: Ethel Mannin is the prolific popular novelist of the working woman: Sounding Brass and Children of the Earth carried the life of the working-class woman into the bestseller, Ragged Banners is her homage to the eccentrics, and Men Are Unwise brought her advanced ideas of marriage to the mountaineering novel of the thirties.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain fast prose of the popular novelist; the working woman of the suburbs and the office; the eccentrics and the road; the anarchist's argument carried in the travel book; the two books a year of the professional writer.
intellectual_concerns: The working-class woman and her life; the suburb and the office; anarchism and anti-fascism; the road and the travel book; the eccentric and the ordinary.
historical_significance: Ethel Mannin is the prolific popular novelist of the working woman: her hundred books made the working woman, the road and the anarchist's argument the matter of the popular literature of the decades.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the criminologist novelist of A Pin to See the Peepshow
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and criminologist; the author of Murder & Its Motives and A Pin to See the Peepshow.
biography: Born Wynifried Margaret Jesse at Chislehurst on 1 March 1888, the granddaughter of Emilia Tennyson and grand-niece of Alfred, Lord Tennyson; she worked as a journalist - reporting the war in Belgium for Collier's - and married the playwright H. M. Harwood in 1918. Under the name F. Tennyson Jesse she wrote the criminology of Murder & Its Motives (1924) and of the Notable British Trials series, and the novels of which The Lacquer Lady (1929) and A Pin to See the Peepshow (1934) are the finest; she died in London on 6 August 1958.
literary_profile: F. Tennyson Jesse is the criminologist's novelist: Murder & Its Motives made the six motives of the killer the framework of the modern criminology, and A Pin to See the Peepshow - the fictional Thompson-Bywaters case - is the classic novel of the woman on trial that the century's revival of her work turned on.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain exact prose of the criminologist; the case, the evidence and the motive reported in the novel; the empire's Burma in the historical novel; the woman on trial and the press; the trial narrative as the moral form.
intellectual_concerns: The murder case and the motives of the killer; the woman on trial and the public; the empire and Burma; the Tennyson family and the literary inheritance; the trial as the narrative of the century.
historical_significance: F. Tennyson Jesse is the criminologist's novelist: Murder & Its Motives framed the modern criminology and A Pin to See the Peepshow is the classic novel of the woman on trial.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the West End dramatist of The Dark River
literary_identity: Playwright and screenwriter; the author of Strange Orchestra and The Dark River.
biography: Born Norman Ackland Bernstein at Westcliff-on-Sea in 1908, the son of the musical comedy star Ada Rodney; he trained at the Central School of Speech Training and wrote his first play, Improper People, at fifteen - it was staged at the Arts Theatre in 1929. Strange Orchestra (1932) was Gielgud's first contemporary play in the West End, After October (1936) is his most autobiographical, and The Dark River (1937), with Peggy Ashcroft, was called on its revival the one indisputably great play of the half-century; he also wrote screenplays with Rattigan; he died on 6 December 1991.
literary_profile: Rodney Ackland is the neglected master of the between-wars West End: The Dark River set the idle household of the Thames backwater against the Spanish war and the coming of fascism with a Chekhovian exactness, and its revivals have made him the rediscovered dramatist of the thirties stage.
stylistic_characteristics: The drawing-room dialogue of the West End with the politics of the decade beneath it; the household cut off in the English countryside; the bohemian family of After October; the film script's pace; the contrast of the frivolous and the responsible in the same scene.
intellectual_concerns: The coming war and the household that ignores it; the English countryside as the refuge and the trap; the bohemian life of the writer; the West End stage and the repertory; the rediscovery of the neglected play.
historical_significance: Rodney Ackland is the neglected master of the between-wars West End: The Dark River set the idle household against the Spanish war with a Chekhovian exactness, and its revivals made him the rediscovered dramatist of the thirties stage.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the working-class essayist of The Freedom of the Streets
literary_identity: Essayist and novelist; the working-class voice of the Adelphi and of The Freedom of the Streets.
biography: Born Jack Common at Heaton, Newcastle, on 15 August 1903, the son of a railway worker; he worked at the trades of the north before moving to London at twenty-five, where he became assistant editor of the Adelphi in the 1930s and acting editor of the New Adelphi in 1936. The essays of The Freedom of the Streets (1938) drew Orwell's praise as the authentic voice of the ordinary working man; his autobiographical novels Kiddar's Luck (1951) and The Ampersand (1954) came after the period and failed commercially; he died at Newport Pagnell on 20 January 1968.
literary_profile: Jack Common is the working-class essayist of the thirties: The Freedom of the Streets carried the voice of the trenches, the sweatshop and the jail into the literary essay, and made him - in Orwell's and Pritchett's judgement - the authentic voice of the ordinary working man of the decade.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain northern prose of the street and the workshop; the essay of the working life in the literary magazine; the argument of the self-taught man; the Newcastle of the terraces and the railway yards; the freedom of the streets against the culture of the comfortable.
intellectual_concerns: The working class and its own voice; the north-east and its industries; the Adelphi and the literary magazine; the self-taught man and his education; the freedom of the streets.
historical_significance: Jack Common is the working-class essayist of the thirties: The Freedom of the Streets made him, in Orwell's judgement, the authentic voice of the ordinary working man of the decade.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Marxist critic of Illusion and Reality, killed at Jarama
literary_identity: Critic and poet; the Marxist aesthete of Illusion and Reality and Studies in a Dying Culture.
biography: Born Christopher St John Sprigg at Putney on 20 October 1907; he left school at fifteen, worked in Fleet Street and wrote aviation books and thrillers under the Sprigg name before joining the Communist Party in 1935 and becoming Christopher Caudwell. Illusion and Reality (1937), the Marxist study of the sources of poetry, appeared in his last year; he drove an ambulance in Spain and was killed at the Jarama in February 1937, leaving the essays of Studies in a Dying Culture (1938) to be published after his death.
literary_profile: Christopher Caudwell is the Marxist critic of the dying culture: Illusion and Reality made the sources of poetry a study of the economics of the imagination, and Studies in a Dying Culture carried the critique of the bourgeois culture to the freedom, the psychology and the law - all written before he was twenty-nine and killed at the Jarama.
stylistic_characteristics: The essay of the argument in the plain Marxist prose; the poetry read through the economics of the society; the dying culture diagnosed in its institutions; the thriller's craft carried into the criticism; the speed of the young mind at work.
intellectual_concerns: Marxism and the aesthetics of the thirties; the poetry and its sources in the society; the dying culture and its institutions; Spain and the generation that went; the young critic killed at twenty-nine.
historical_significance: Christopher Caudwell is the Marxist critic of the dying culture: Illusion and Reality made the sources of poetry a study of the economics of the imagination, written before he was killed at the Jarama at twenty-nine.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Communist critic of The Novel and the People, killed in Spain
literary_identity: Critic, journalist and novelist; the Communist writer of Storm over England and The Novel and the People.
biography: Born Ralph Winston Fox at Leeds in 1900; he read modern languages at Oxford, worked as a journalist and for the Comintern, and wrote for the Daily Worker through the thirties. Storm over England (1935) told the three centuries of the English class war, The Colonial Policy of British Imperialism (1933) made the Marxist case against the empire, and The Novel and the People (1937) was published after he was killed fighting in Spain in the winter of 1936-7.
literary_profile: Ralph Fox is the Communist critic of the people's novel: The Novel and the People made the case for the novel as the literature of the people and against the dying bourgeois form, and his death in Spain made him, with Caudwell and Cornford, one of the martyrs of the thirties left.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain argumentative prose of the Communist journalist; the class war told as the history of the people; the novel judged by its service to the people; the colonial critique of the empire; the pamphlet's speed and conviction.
intellectual_concerns: The class war and the English history; the empire and its colonial policy; the novel and the people; Spain and the thirties left; the martyrdom of the Communist writers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the weird tale's architect of the Cthulhu Mythos
literary_identity: Writer of the weird tale; the creator of the Cthulhu Mythos and of the cosmic horror.
biography: Born Howard Phillips Lovecraft at Providence, Rhode Island, on 20 August 1890; he grew up in the antiquarian Providence of his grandfather's library, wrote for the amateur press, and from 1923 made the weird tale of the pulps - The Colour Out of Space (1927), The Call of Cthulhu (1928), At the Mountains of Madness (1936) and The Shadow over Innsmouth (1936) - into the cosmic horror of the indifferent universe. He died at Providence, in poverty, on 15 March 1937, and the mythos he built became the foundation of the modern weird tale.
literary_profile: H. P. Lovecraft is the architect of the modern weird tale: the Cthulhu Mythos made the horror of the cosmos - the indifferent universe, the buried gods, the degenerate town - the matter of the pulp tale, and his influence on the horror and the science fiction of the later century is unmatched by any writer of the pulps.
stylistic_characteristics: The antiquarian prose of the report and the manuscript; the adjectives of the unnameable and the geometry that is not Euclidean; the New England of the decayed port and the haunted hill; the cosmic indifference in place of the ghost's malice; the tale told as the document of the scholar.
intellectual_concerns: The cosmic horror and the indifferent universe; the mythos of the buried gods; the decayed New England town; the scholar's document and the forbidden book; the weird tale of the pulps.
historical_significance: H. P. Lovecraft is the architect of the modern weird tale: the Cthulhu Mythos made the cosmic horror of the indifferent universe the matter of the pulp tale, and his influence on the later horror is unmatched.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the novelist of Darkness at Noon and the testament of Spain
literary_identity: Novelist and political writer; the author of Spanish Testament and Darkness at Noon.
biography: Born Artúr Kösztler at Budapest on 5 September 1905; he worked as a journalist in Palestine and Berlin, joined the Communist Party in 1931, and was imprisoned by the Francoists in Spain, the experience of Spanish Testament (1937). Leaving the party, he wrote Darkness at Noon (1940), the great novel of the Moscow trials, in German and had it translated by Daphne Hardy; Arrival and Departure (1943) carried the war's refugees into the novel of the psychoanalysis. He took his own life in London on 1 March 1983.
literary_profile: Arthur Koestler is the novelist of the totalitarian century: Darkness at Noon made Rubashov's cell and its confession the definitive novel of the show trials, and Spanish Testament is the testimony of the party's disillusion in the decade of the Popular Front.
stylistic_characteristics: The argument carried in the cell and the interrogation; the plain analytical prose of the political mind; the confession as the moral problem; the refugee's war in the psychoanalytic novel; the essay and the testament beside the fiction.
intellectual_concerns: Totalitarianism and the show trial; the party and the disillusion; the Spain of the Popular Front; the refugee and the war; the confession and the conscience of the revolutionary.
